Twins
twĭnz
n. pl. (two born at one birth; in Genesis the setting for the doctrine of election)
Old English getwinn, twofold. Hebrew teom, a twin — the root behind the name Thomas, called Didymus, the twin.

Biblical Definition

Twins are born twice in Genesis and both times the birth carries doctrine. Of Rebekah: “when her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb” (Gen 25:24), of whom the LORD had already said, “Two nations are in thy womb… and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen 25:23). Of Tamar: “in the time of her travail, that, behold, twins were in her womb” (Gen 38:27). The Song uses the word for beauty and abundance — teeth like a flock “whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them” (Son 4:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a twin as one of two young produced at a birth by an animal that ordinarily brings forth but one, and as an adjective, born at the same birth.

expand to see more

TWIN, n. One of two young produced at a birth by an animal that usually brings forth but one.

TWIN, a. Noting two born at a birth; as twin brothers.

TWIN, a. Very much resembling; as twin virtues.

Key Scripture

Gen 25:23 — "And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger."

Gen 25:24 — "And when her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb."

Gen 38:27 — "And it came to pass in the time of her travail, that, behold, twins were in her womb."

Son 4:2 — "Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them."

Modern Corruption

Paul builds unconditional election on twins in one womb, because nothing but the purpose of God could distinguish them.

expand to see more

Romans 9 chooses this example on purpose. Jacob and Esau shared a father, a mother, a womb, and a birthday; and God said the elder shall serve the younger before they were born, neither having done any good or evil. Paul draws the conclusion himself: that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth. Every ground of distinction that men reach for is removed by the circumstances of the case. If God's choice rested on foreseen faith, foreseen works, or foreseen anything, Genesis 25:23 was spoken too early. Unconditional election is not a doctrine imposed on this text; it is the reason the text is written the way it is.

The corruption to name is the reading that makes Romans 9 about nations rather than persons, so that election becomes a matter of historical roles and not of salvation. Paul will not permit the escape: he moves from Jacob and Esau to Pharaoh to vessels of mercy prepared unto glory, and answers the objection any honest reader raises — why doth he yet find fault? — not by softening the doctrine but by asking who the objector is. The corporate reading is offered as a kindness to God's reputation. God does not need it, and Paul does not use it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew teom (H8380), twin; Greek Didumos (G1324), Didymus, the twin; Greek ekloge (G1589), election, choosing out.

expand to see more

Hebrew teom (H8380) — twin; Genesis 25:24, 38:27, Song of Solomon 4:2.

Greek Didumos (G1324) — Didymus, twin; John 11:16, 20:24, 21:2.

Greek ekloge (G1589) — election, the act of choosing; Romans 9:11, 11:5, 2 Peter 1:10.

Hebrew rab / tsair — the elder, the younger; Genesis 25:23.

Hebrew beten (H990) — belly, womb; Genesis 25:23, Psalm 139:13.

Usage

"“Behold, there were twins in her womb” — Rebekah delivered."

"“The elder shall serve the younger” — spoken before they were born."

"“Every one bear twins, and none is barren” — the Song's figure of fruitfulness."
